sayadaws.name: Ven. Mogok Sayadaw (U Vimala)
sayadaws.biography: Master exponent of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) applied directly to contemplative insight, emphasizing discernment of arising and passing away of consciousness (citta) to sever craving (taṇhā).

discourses.title: Part 05-02: Stopping and Contemplation (Samatha & Vipassanā Turning Point)
discourses.sourceText: Dhamma Talks by Mogok Sayadaw (Part 5, Talk 2)
discourses.summary: Ven. Mogok Sayadaw explains how halting outward proliferation and turning awareness immediately onto arising-and-passing mental and bodily phenomena transforms ordinary experience into liberating insight.

sections.heading: 1. Stopping the Stream of Proliferation
paragraphs: When the eye sees a visible form or the ear hears a sound, the untrained mind immediately runs outward in pursuit of stories, judgments, and desires. Mogok Sayadaw compares this habit to a traveler running blindly down a slope without ever pausing to inspect where each step lands.

"Stopping" (samatha in its practical sense) begins the moment you refuse to follow the story. Instead of adding a second thought of liking or disliking onto the first contact, you steady the mind right at the point of awareness. In that pause, restlessness settles and clarity becomes possible.

sections.heading: 2. Contemplating Arising and Passing Away
paragraphs: Stopping alone is not yet the end of the path; it prepares the clear mirror for contemplation (vipassanā). Once the mind stops chasing external concepts, turn attention directly to the consciousness or sensation currently present—hearing, thinking, warmth, tightness, or pleasant feeling.

Watch carefully: did that state stay permanent even for two heartbeats? No—it arose from conditions and vanished right where it stood. When you directly discern impermanence (anicca) in the present mind-and-matter process, ignorance loses its footing and craving cannot bind the heart.

discourses.pullQuote: Do not chase what has already vanished, and do not welcome what has not yet arrived. Stop right here and contemplate the phenomenon before your eyes.

tips.title: Establishing a Gentle Anchor at the Abdomen or Nostrils
tips.authorSayadaw: Ven. Mahāsi Sayadaw & Ven. Pa-Auk Sayadaw
tips.summary: Observe the natural movement of breathing without controlling its depth or speed, letting awareness rest softly on physical sensations.
guidance: Sit upright with relaxed shoulders and let the eyes close gently. Do not force a deep breath or alter the natural rhythm of the body.
Direct attention either to the rising and falling sensation at the abdomen (Mahāsi method) or to the tactile touch of air at the rim of the nostrils (Ānāpānasati).
Whenever the mind wanders into planning or memory, note "wandering" or "thinking" gently without frustration, and return calmly to the very next breath.

tips.title: Walking Meditation Cadence: Lifting, Moving, Placing
tips.summary: Alternating sitting and walking meditation keeps energy balanced, prevents dullness, and trains continuity of mindfulness in motion.
guidance: Choose a quiet straight path of 10 to 15 paces. Stand still for a few breaths, feeling the uprightness and weight of the body.
Walk at a measured, unhurried pace. Keep your gaze lowered a few feet ahead and notice the changing sensations of lightness, movement, and contact in each step.
At the end of the path, pause to notice "standing," turn slowly with clear awareness of the turning motion, and resume walking smoothly.

tips.title: Meeting Restlessness, Drowsiness, and Doubt Without Resistance
tips.summary: Hindrances are not failures of meditation; when observed objectively as temporary mental states, they become objects of insight.
guidance: When sleepiness (thīna-middha) clouds awareness, straighten the spine, breathe slightly more briskly for three cycles, or switch to brisk walking meditation.
When restlessness or worry (uddhacca-kukkucca) agitates the mind, stop fighting the thoughts. Recognize the agitated mind itself as an impermanent mental event arising and passing away.
Remember Mogok Sayadaw’s reminder: you do not need to erase yesterday’s thoughts—simply observe the present mental state clearly so craving cannot feed it.

tips.title: Carrying Clear Comprehension Into Daily Transitions
tips.summary: Bridge formal cushion practice with ordinary responsibilities by pausing at natural thresholds throughout the day.
guidance: Use everyday transitions—standing up from a chair, opening a door, washing hands, or taking the first spoonful of a meal—as quiet bells for mindfulness.
Notice the intention just before acting (cetanā) and the bodily sensations as the movement unfolds.
End each evening with five minutes of reflecting on wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, cultivating mettā toward all beings.

events.title: 10-Day Satipaṭṭhāna Vipassanā Course
events.locationOrLink: Group Retreat Hall · Main Dhamma Sanctuary
events.teacher: Ven. Dr. Nandamālābhivaṃsa & Senior Assistant Sayadaw
events.description: Ten-day intensive retreat following the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta with alternating sitting and walking periods, evening Abhidhamma & Vipassanā discourses, and daily teacher interviews.

events.title: Weekly Sunday Group Sitting & Abhidhamma Study
events.description: One-hour silent Vipassanā sitting followed by 30 minutes of walking meditation, chanting of the Mettā Sutta, and guided reading from Fundamental Abhidhamma.

events.title: Practical Paṭiccasamuppāda Seminar (Mogok Tradition)
events.description: Focused afternoon discourse and Q&A exploring how contemplation of consciousness (cittānupassanā) severs the link between feeling (vedanā) and craving (taṇhā).

events.title: Full-Moon Uposatha One-Day Mindfulness Retreat
events.description: One-day Eight Precepts observance with guided Ānāpānasati sitting, mindful vegetarian lunch, and group sutta recitation.
